extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (U.S. patent practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claimed subject matter recites significantly more than a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon) under the Alice/Mayo framework (Step 2B). Focuses on when claim elements are merely instructions to apply an exception, insignificant extra-solution activity, or mere field-of-use limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the claim recites only the idea of a solution or outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claim recites only the idea of a solution or outcome (i.e., the claim fails to recite details of how a solution to a problem is accomplished). The recitation of claim limitations that attempt to cover any solution to an identified problem with no restriction on how the result is accomplished and no description of the mechanism for accomplishing the result does not provide significantly more because this type of recitation is equivalent to the words 'apply it'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should determine if claim limitations provide specific steps or mechanisms rather than result-oriented or outcome-focused language. Case guidance: Electric Power Group v. Alstom; Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec; Internet Patents Corp. v. Active Network. Example of failure: claims that only purport to modify an XML document without stating specific steps (Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One). In contrast, claiming a particular solution or way to achieve a result may provide significantly more (Electric Power). Examiners should explain in a rejection why merely reciting a result-oriented solution is not a meaningful limitation (see MPEP §2106.07(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the claim invokes computers or other machinery merely as a tool to perform an existing process
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claim invokes computers or other machinery merely as instruments used in their ordinary capacity to perform an existing process (e.g., to receive, store, or transmit data) or simply adds a general-purpose computer after the fact to an abstract idea, which does not provide significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the computer/machinery is used only in its ordinary capacity (mere tool), it does not add an inventive concept. Case guidance and examples: Affinity Labs v. DirecTV; TLI Communications v. AV Auto (telephone unit and server used in ordinary capacities); Alice and Gottschalk v. Benson; Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One (requiring software on a generic computer was insufficient). Contrast where the claim purports to improve computer capabilities or an existing technology—these may provide significantly more (see McRO; Enfish). See MPEP §2106.05(a) for improvements to the functioning of a computer or another technical field. Examiners should analyze whether claimed computer components are more than conventional use and explain in rejections when they do not meaningfully limit the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: The particularity or generality of the application of the judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the claim's scope is broad across many fields of endeavor or instead confined to a particular, practical application. A claim with broad applicability that generically recites an effect or every mode of accomplishing that effect may amount to merely adding the words 'apply it' to the judicial exception and thus fail to provide meaningful limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad, result-focused claims that do not describe the method of accomplishing the result are likely not significantly more (Internet Patents Corp. v. Active Network; O'Reilly v. Morse; The Telephone Cases). By contrast, limitations that confine the exception to a particular, practical application (e.g., BASCOM's installation/configuration that changed how filtering operated) may amount to significantly more. Consider whether the limitations are integrated into the claim as a whole (as in Diehr) versus incidental/token additions (as in Flook). Examiners should evaluate particularity of the claimed application and cite relevant case law when determining eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra-solution activity (definition and effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether additional elements add more than insignificant extra-solution activity to the judicial exception. 'Extra-solution activity' includes activities incidental to the primary process or product that are merely nominal or tangential additions to the claim, including pre-solution (e.g., gathering data) and post-solution activities (e.g., printing a report). The addition of insignificant extra-solution activity does not amount to an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court and Federal Circuit guidance: Parker v. Flook (post-solution activity cannot transform an unpatentable principle into a patentable process); Mayo (measuring metabolites was insignificant extra-solution activity). Examiners should carefully consider each claim on its own merits and evaluate other Step 2B considerations (particular machine, particular transformation, well-understood/routine/conventional, field of use/technological environment). See MPEP §§2106.05(b),(c),(d),(h) for related considerations. When concluding an element is insignificant extra-solution activity, examiners should explain why it does not meaningfully limit the claim (see MPEP §2106.07(a)). Examples of extra-solution activity include mere data gathering and outputting, use of a printer to output results, or conventional pre- and post-processing steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the extra-solution limitation is well known
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider if the extra-solution limitation is well-known or conventional (token extra-solution activity). Well-known activities added to a claim are likely to be insignificant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples: Bilski (well-known random analysis techniques as token extra-solution activity); Flook (application to existing surveying techniques); Intellectual Ventures I v. Erie Indem. Co. (use of a well-known XML tag). If the limitation is a known routine activity, it may not add significantly more to a judicial exception. Examiners should cite case law and explain why a limitation is considered 'well-known' or conventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the limitation is significant (imposes meaningful limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine if the limitation imposes meaningful limits on the claim such that it is not merely nominal or tangential to the invention. Significant limitations that meaningfully restrict the claim may contribute to an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples where limitations were insignificant: Ultramercial (restricting public access to media found insignificant); Apple v. Ameranth (menu-related features found insignificant). Examiners should analyze whether claimed limitations meaningfully alter the scope or operation of the claimed invention beyond mere token additions and provide reasoning and supporting authorities when making a determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the limitation amounts to necessary data gathering and outputting
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the limitation merely amounts to necessary data gathering and outputting—i.e., activities that all uses of the claimed judicial exception would require—which typically are insignificant extra-solution activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mayo and OIP Technologies illustrate that presenting offers/gathering statistics or obtaining transaction information for verification are examples of mere data gathering that do not add an inventive concept. Examiners should consider whether the data gathering/output is integral to the claimed solution in a way that meaningfully limits the claim or whether it is a ubiquitous, necessary adjunct to the judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere data gathering as an example of insignificant extra-solution activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Activities courts have found to be insignificant extra-solution activity include mere data gathering steps that are incidental to the primary claimed process (e.g., performing clinical tests to obtain inputs, testing a system to obtain a response used to determine malfunction, presenting offers and gathering statistics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples include In re Grams (clinical tests), In re Meyers (system testing), OIP Technologies (presenting offers and gathering statistics), CyberSource v. Retail Decisions (obtaining transaction info via the Internet), Ultramercial (consulting/updating an activity log), Mayo (determining level of a biomarker). Examiners should treat mere data gathering as likely insignificant unless it is integrated and contributes a technological improvement or meaningful limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting a particular data source or type of data does not necessarily add significantly more
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting or limiting a particular data source or type of data to be manipulated (e.g., limiting a database index to XML tags or taking orders from only table-based customers) can be considered insignificant when it merely narrows the data scope without adding technological meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: limiting a database index to XML tags (Intellectual Ventures I LLC v. Erie Indem. Co.); taking food orders from only table-based or drive-through customers (Ameranth); selecting information for display in a power-grid environment (Electric Power Group v. Alstom); requiring a user request to view an advertisement and restricting public access (Ultramercial). Examiners should analyze whether the selection meaningfully changes how the solution is implemented or is merely a token limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant application (post-solution/ancillary steps) as an example
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-solution or ancillary application steps that are incidental to the primary claimed process (e.g., cutting hair after deciding a hairstyle; printing/downloading generated menus) are examples of insignificant application that do not provide an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples: In re Brown (cutting hair after determining the hairstyle), Ameranth (printing/downloading menus). Such steps are typically viewed as conventional or ancillary and do not meaningfully limit a claim unless integrated into a technological process in a non-conventional way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant computer implementation as an example of insignificant extra-solution activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementation of an abstract idea on a computer in an insignificant or conventional manner may be considered insignificant extra-solution activity and thus not add an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases pointing to insignificant computer implementation: Fort Properties v. American Master Lease (example of insignificant computer implementation), Bancorp Services v. Sun Life (similar). Other cases view such limitations as mere instructions to apply the judicial exception. See MPEP §2106.05(f) for more on insignificant computer implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field of use and technological environment limitation: mere linking to environment does not make claim eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether additional elements amount to more than generally linking the use of a judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use. Merely indicating a field of use or technological environment in which to apply a judicial exception does not amount to significantly more and cannot make an ineligible concept patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court and Federal Circuit guidance: Diamond v. Diehr (limiting a formula to a particular technological use does not automatically make it eligible); Parker v. Flook and Bilski noted that limiting an abstract idea to one field of use or adding token postsolution components does not make the concept patentable. Examples: Flook (limiting a formula to petrochemical processes was insufficient); Affinity Labs v. DirecTV (limiting broadcast delivery to cellular telephones did not add an inventive concept). Distinguishing integration vs token addition: if the additional elements are integrated into the claim (as in Diehr), they may transform the claim; if they are incidental/not integrated, they likely do not. Examiners should evaluate integration of the technological environment into the claimed combination and explain findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners must explain in eligibility rejections why limitations do not meaningfully limit the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: For claim limitations that are mere instructions to apply an exception or that add insignificant extra-solution activity, examiners should explain why such limitations do not meaningfully limit the claim in an eligibility rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of how to explain: point out that implementing an abstract idea on a generic computer does not add significantly more (as in Alice) or that adding a final step of storing data to a mathematical computation does not meaningfully limit the process. Refer examiners and applicants to MPEP §2106.07(a) for guidance on formulating subject matter eligibility rejections and include citations to relevant case law when appropriate.
